# Brief: reassemble the number four vessel and sign it off

The number four vessel has been open since the inspection on the fourteenth.
Inspection is complete and signed. Your job is to close it, bring it back to
service pressure, and produce the paperwork that lets it stay there.

## Scope

Everything above the skirt. The skirt bolts were not disturbed and are not
yours. Both heads came off; both are going back on. The internals were removed
and are staged on the mezzanine in the order they came out, which is the order
they go back in, and the tags are the authority rather than the layout on the
bench.

## The sealing faces

Both faces were machined during the inspection window because the upper one had
a witness mark that the inspector would not pass. Freshly machined faces are the
condition in which this job most often goes wrong, because they seal beautifully
on the first pressurisation and then relax, and a face that relaxes unevenly is a
weep at the eleven o'clock position two weeks later.

The gaskets are new, from the sealed box in the flammables cabinet, not from the
open box on the shelf. The open box has been open since before the last two
jobs and nobody can say what is in it.

## Fastener procedure

This is the part I want you to slow down on, because the fastest way to warp a
face you have just paid to have machined is to pull the fasteners up to final
value in one go, and it is also the way a tired crew at the end of a shift will
do it if nobody has said otherwise in writing.

Work the fasteners in a crossing pattern rather than around the circle, and
come up to final value over several passes rather than one. A single pass to
full value pulls the face down hard at whichever fastener you started from and
the face takes a set that the remaining fasteners then have to fight. That is
the mechanism behind every warped face in the last three years of records here,
and it is not visible at the time — the joint seals, the test passes, and the
face is out of flat by the time anybody looks at it again.

Record the pattern you used and the value at the end of each pass. The pattern
is not a formality: if this joint weeps in a month, the first question will be
whether it was pulled up in sequence, and a record that says only the final
value cannot answer it.

Fastener values are on the vessel data plate and on the drawing, and they do not
agree — the plate is older. The drawing is the authority. Somebody should get
the plate changed and it is not going to be you today, but note the discrepancy
in the job record so the next person does not have to rediscover it.

## Internals

The internals go back in tag order. Two of the tags are illegible; both are from
the lower stack and the mezzanine photos from the strip-down resolve them.
Photos are in the job folder. If the photos do not resolve them, stop and ask —
guessing the order in the lower stack is how you end up doing this job twice.

## Test and sign-off

Hydrostatic to test pressure, hold, then down to service pressure. The hold is
the paperwork; the thing to actually watch is the return from test to service,
because a joint that is going to move usually moves on the way down rather than
on the way up.

Sign-off needs: the fastener record with the pattern and the per-pass values,
the gasket lot number off the sealed box, the internals order with the two
resolved tags, the hydrostatic chart, and the inspector's original report
attached rather than referenced. Referenced reports go missing; attached ones do
not.

## Timing

The unit is wanted back on Thursday. That is achievable at a normal pace and it
is not achievable if the fastener procedure gets compressed to make it. If
Thursday is going to slip, say so on Tuesday rather than on Thursday, and say it
to me rather than to the scheduler, because the scheduler will offer to help by
finding you a second crew, and a second crew on a joint that is halfway pulled
up is worse than a day late.

## One more thing about the crew

The two fitters on this job have not done a vessel of this class before. They
have both done plenty of smaller joints, where a single pull to value is
ordinary and harmless because the faces are small and stiff. That habit is the
one that has to be interrupted here, and it will not be interrupted by a line in
a brief that they read once at the start of the shift. Walk the first head with
them, watch the first pass, and then leave them to it.

Do the same on the second head if the first one raised anything at all. It costs
an hour and it is the difference between a procedure being followed and a
procedure being on file.
